ety.text: From Middle English ells, elles, from Old English elles (“other, otherwise, different”), from Proto-West Germanic *alljas, from Proto-Germanic *aljas (“of another, of something else”), genitive of *aljaz (“other”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élyos, from *h₂el- (“other”).

senses.d: Other; in addition to previously mentioned items.
ex: The instructor is busy. Can anyone else help me?
Whatever else she may be, she is not a surgeon.
How else (= in what other way) can it be done?
I'm busy Friday; when else (= what other time) works for you?
Then the Wronskian of f and g must be nonzero, else they could not be linearly independent.

grp.label: word that implies any result with the exception of the one being referred to
for otherwise — see also or else

chain.g: more, the more, in a greater measure, to a greater extent

ety.text: Inherited from Latin magis. Consider also derivative Latin magister, whence English master.

pt:mais.gl: used to form the comparative of adjectives and adverbs; more; -er

ety.text: From Old Galician-Portuguese mais, from Latin magis (“more”). Doublet of mas. Displaced collateral form chus.
Contraction of Middle French si non. Compare Catalan sinó, Portuguese senão, and Romanesco "sinnò".

fr:autrement.gl: differently, in another way or manner

ety.text: From Middle French aultrement, from Old French autrement, from Early Medieval Latin alterā mente. Synchronically autre + -ment.
Inherited from Latin alterum, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élteros.
Borrowed from Latin signum. Doublet of signo, cf. also seña. Cognate with English sign.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese senon. By surface analysis, se (“if”) + não (“not”). Compare French sinon, Spanish sino.

pt:em vez de.gl: instead of; in lieu of; in place of; rather than

pt:além disso.gl: in addition, moreover, besides, furthermore, to boot (in addition to what has been said)

ety.text: From Middle English elswher, from Old English elles hwǣr and elles hwerġen (“elsewhere”); corresponding with else + where. Cognate with Old High German alleswār (“elsewhere”), whence Middle High German alleswā, alswā (“elsewhere”).

senses.d: Synonym of somewhere else: in, at, or to some other place.
ex: If you won’t serve us, we’ll go elsewhere.
These particular trees are not to be found elsewhere.

senses.d: Synonym of somewhere else: a place other than here.
ex: We are back on the Ligurian coast, from which vertigos push human beings toward all kinds of elsewheres.

chain.g: to another place, in another direction, elsewhere

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French ailleurs, from Old French aillors, aillurs (“elsewhere”), probably from Latin aliōrsum, or from a Vulgar Latin *aliore, from in *aliore loco. Possibly connected to Latin aliubī, from alibī. Compare with Occitan alhors, Portuguese alhures and Romanian aiurea.
